title: The foundations
hook: the preliminary practices: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga

segments.voice: Yesterday, prostrations, the whole body to the ground. Your line was all the way down. Did your shoulders drop, even once? Day one thousand three hundred five.

Nobody stops on the sidewalk to admire a foundation. It's poured first, it's underground, and by the time anyone visits, it's covered over with floors and furniture. But build a house without one and the house will tell you. Doors stick. Cracks run up the walls. Tibetan Buddhism has a name for the work that goes under everything else, the part nobody photographs and some practitioners spend years on. Yesterday's bow was the first piece of it. Today's word is the whole foundation: ngondro.
screen: `NOBODY ADMIRES A FOUNDATION.` → `WITHOUT ONE, THE HOUSE TELLS YOU.` → `NGONDRO.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ngondro is Tibetan, usually translated as the preliminaries: the practices that come before. Before what? Before the deeper meditations a teacher may give later. But before doesn't mean less. Second, the four. Refuge and prostration: going to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, with the body bowing all the way down. Purification: the mantra of Vajrasattva, for washing away past wrongs. The mandala offering: giving away the whole world, pictured on a plate of rice. And guru yoga: joining your mind with the teacher's awakened mind. Each of these gets its own day this week, so today is just the map. Third, schools build it differently. In some lineages the ngondro opens with four thoughts that turn the mind toward practice: the preciousness of a human life, impermanence, karma, and the suffering of the round. Other schools arrange their preliminaries in their own order, with their own lists. Tradition sets each practice at a large number of repetitions, and people often complete them slowly, around jobs and families, over a long time. Fourth, why the foundation matters so much. A saying heard in Tibetan teaching puts it boldly: the preliminaries are more profound than the main practice. Some teachers go back to them again and again, long after finishing. A foundation isn't the part you outgrow. It's the part everything else is standing on.
screen: `NGONDRO: WHAT COMES BEFORE.` · `REFUGE, PURIFICATION, OFFERING, GURU.` · `SCHOOLS BUILD IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `NOT OUTGROWN, STOOD ON.` · then, large: `THE FOUNDATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the four, one at each corner. Sit comfortably and picture a plain square slab of foundation, seen from above. Breathe in, and set the first practice at one corner: refuge and prostration. Breathe out. The next corner: purification. The third: the offering. The fourth: guru yoga. Then walk around the square again, slower, letting each one sit for a moment. You don't need to do any of them. Just know where each one stands. When the square feels steady, let the picture go and rest in the plain breath under it, the way a house rests on what's underneath. The bell holds the time.
Ngondro. The preliminaries, the foundations of Tibetan practice: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga. Today's word.
Your line: the foundations. Today, notice one boring, basic thing that holds your life up, sleep, a meal, a friend's call, and give it some respect. Day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist students complete the ngondro under a teacher's guidance, doing refuge with prostrations, Vajrasattva purification, the mandala offering and guru yoga, often over years and alongside ordinary life.
